species.name: Beef
species.nameNeverSays: A cut name says where on the animal the meat comes from. It doesn’t say the breed, the USDA grade, what the animal ate, where it was raised, or who processed it — check the label for those.

species.name: Pork
species.nameNeverSays: A cut name says where on the animal the meat comes from. It doesn’t say the breed, how the pig was raised or housed, what it ate, or where — check the label for those.

species.name: Chicken
species.nameNeverSays: A part name says which piece of the bird it is. It doesn’t say how the bird was raised, its age, or where it came from — check the label for those (and the USDA class name, such as Broiler or Roaster).

primals.name: Chuck
primals.about: The shoulder and neck. Hard-working muscle: rich flavor, more connective tissue.

primals.name: Rib
primals.about: Ribs six through twelve along the back. Tender, well-marbled cuts.

primals.name: Short loin
primals.about: The middle of the back behind the rib. The most tender steaks.

primals.name: Sirloin
primals.about: The back between the short loin and the round. Lean, fairly tender.

primals.name: Round
primals.about: The rear leg. Lean, firm muscle.

primals.name: Brisket
primals.about: The lower chest below the chuck.

primals.name: Plate
primals.about: The belly below the rib, behind the brisket.

primals.name: Flank
primals.about: The belly below the loin, in front of the rear leg.

primals.name: Shank
primals.about: The lower legs. Very lean, lots of connective tissue.

primals.name: Jowl
primals.about: The cheek and jaw.

primals.name: Shoulder butt
primals.about: The upper shoulder (Boston butt). Well-marbled.

primals.name: Picnic shoulder
primals.about: The lower shoulder and front leg.

primals.name: Loin
primals.about: The back from shoulder to hip. Chops, roasts, tenderloin, back ribs.

primals.name: Belly (side)
primals.about: The underside below the loin. Bacon and spare ribs.

primals.name: Leg (ham)
primals.about: The hind leg.

primals.name: Breast
primals.about: The chest muscle. White meat.

primals.name: Wing
primals.about: The wing: drumette, flat and tip.

primals.name: Thigh
primals.about: The upper leg. Dark meat.

primals.name: Drumstick
primals.about: The lower leg. Dark meat.

primals.name: Whole leg
primals.about: Thigh and drumstick together.

primals.name: Back
primals.about: The backbone and ribs. Mostly used for stock.

primals.name: Whole bird
primals.about: The whole carcass.

cuts.name: Ribeye
cuts.about: A steak from the rib section, cut from the large eye muscle (longissimus) and the cap around it. Sold boneless or bone-in.
cuts.nameNote: “Delmonico” is used for more than one cut — some butchers mean a ribeye, others a strip or a chuck-eye steak. Ask which.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 100 (beef); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Bone-in ribeye (cowboy, tomahawk)
cuts.about: A ribeye with the rib bone left on. A tomahawk keeps a long, cleaned (frenched) bone; a cowboy steak has a shorter one.
cuts.nameNote: The bone adds weight to the price. The meat is the same ribeye.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 100 (beef); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Prime rib (standing rib roast)
cuts.about: A roast from the rib section, usually bone-in, sliced to order.
cuts.nameNote: “Prime rib” is the name of the roast, not a USDA grade. It need not be USDA Prime — ask what grade it is.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 100 (beef); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Ribeye cap (spinalis)
cuts.about: The curved outer muscle of the ribeye, removed and sold on its own. Very marbled.
cuts.nameNote: “Deckle” is also used for part of the brisket — ask which.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 100 (beef); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Short ribs
cuts.about: Rib bones with the meat between them. Most come from the plate; “chuck short ribs” come from the chuck and some from the rib. Flanken and LA galbi are cut across the bones; English-cut runs along one bone.
cuts.nameNote: “Short rib” doesn’t say which section — plate, chuck or rib — and they differ in meat and fat.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 100 (beef); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Strip steak (New York strip)
cuts.about: A steak from the short loin, cut from the same long muscle as the ribeye but farther back. Leaner, with a firmer bite.
cuts.nameNote: New York, Kansas City and top loin are the same cut; the city in the name isn’t where the beef came from.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 100 (beef); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: T-bone
cuts.about: A bone-in steak from the short loin with strip on one side of the T-shaped bone and a small piece of tenderloin on the other.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 100 (beef); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Porterhouse
cuts.about: A T-bone cut from the rear of the short loin, where the tenderloin side is larger. USDA specs require a wider tenderloin portion than a T-bone.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 100 (beef); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Tenderloin (filet mignon)
cuts.about: The long, very tender muscle under the backbone. It runs from the short loin back into the sirloin. Filet mignon is a steak cut from it; chateaubriand is a thick center-cut roast.
cuts.nameNote: “Filet” alone can mean other cuts (a “filet” of chicken or fish, a “sirloin filet”). “Tenderloin tips” are often trimmings.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 100 (beef); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Top sirloin
cuts.about: A lean steak from the top of the sirloin section.
cuts.nameNote: “Sirloin” alone can mean the top sirloin or cheaper bottom-sirloin cuts.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 100 (beef); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Picanha (top sirloin cap)
cuts.about: The cap muscle on top of the sirloin with its fat layer left on. Popular in Brazilian steakhouses.
cuts.nameNote: In the UK and Australia “rump cap” is the same muscle; in the US “rump roast” means a round cut.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 100 (beef); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Tri-tip
cuts.about: A triangular muscle from the bottom sirloin.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 100 (beef); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Bavette (sirloin flap)
cuts.about: A loose-grained steak from the bottom sirloin, often used for carne asada.
cuts.nameNote: In France “bavette” can also mean a flank steak. “Sirloin tip” is also a round cut — ask which.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 100 (beef); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Top round (London broil)
cuts.about: A large, lean muscle from the inside of the rear leg.
cuts.nameNote: “London broil” is a way of cooking and slicing, not a single cut — it may be top round, flank or another lean cut.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 100 (beef); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Eye of round
cuts.about: A small, very lean, cylinder-shaped muscle from the rear leg. Often thin-sliced for roast beef.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 100 (beef); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Bottom round (rump roast)
cuts.about: A lean muscle from the outside of the rear leg, often braised or roasted.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 100 (beef); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Sirloin tip (knuckle)
cuts.about: Despite the name, a round cut: the front of the rear leg just below the sirloin.
cuts.nameNote: “Sirloin” in the name doesn’t mean it comes from the sirloin.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 100 (beef); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Chuck roast
cuts.about: A shoulder roast with lots of connective tissue that turns tender with slow cooking.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 100 (beef); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Chuck eye steak
cuts.about: A steak from the chuck where it meets the rib, continuing the ribeye’s eye muscle.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 100 (beef); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Flat iron
cuts.about: A tender steak from the top blade muscle of the shoulder, with the center seam of gristle removed.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 100 (beef); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Denver steak
cuts.about: A steak from the underblade muscle of the chuck.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 100 (beef); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Teres major (petite tender)
cuts.about: A small, tender shoulder muscle often compared to tenderloin.
cuts.nameNote: Sold as “petite filet”, but it isn’t tenderloin.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 100 (beef); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Skirt steak
cuts.about: A long, thin, loose-grained steak from the diaphragm (outside skirt) or the inner belly wall (inside skirt). Common for fajitas.
cuts.nameNote: “Fajita meat” may be skirt, flank or other cuts.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 100 (beef); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Hanger steak
cuts.about: A single steak per animal that hangs from the diaphragm beneath the loin.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 100 (beef); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Flank steak
cuts.about: A flat, lean, long-grained steak from the belly below the loin.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 100 (beef); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Brisket
cuts.about: The chest muscles. Sold whole or as the leaner flat (first cut) and fattier point (second cut). Corned beef is usually cured brisket.
cuts.nameNote: “Corned beef” names the cure, not the cut — some is made from round.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 100 (beef); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Shank (osso buco)
cuts.about: Cross-cut slices of the lower leg with marrow bone in the center, for long braising.
cuts.nameNote: Osso buco is traditionally veal shank; a menu may not say which.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 100 (beef); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Pork butt (Boston butt)
cuts.about: The upper part of the shoulder — not the rear. Well-marbled; the usual cut for pulled pork. Sliced, it’s a blade or pork steak.
cuts.nameNote: “Butt” doesn’t mean the rear of the pig. “Pork shoulder” can mean the butt or the picnic.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 400 (pork); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Pork collar (coppa)
cuts.about: The neck-end muscle of the shoulder butt. Cured whole, it’s coppa (capicola).
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 400 (pork); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Picnic shoulder
cuts.about: The lower shoulder and front leg, below the butt. Often sold skin-on or smoked.
cuts.nameNote: A “picnic ham” is shoulder, not ham.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 400 (pork); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Pork loin roast
cuts.about: The long muscle along the back, sold boneless or bone-in as a rack.
cuts.nameNote: Pork loin and pork tenderloin are different muscles.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 400 (pork); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Pork chop
cuts.about: A slice of the loin. Rib chops come from the shoulder end, loin and porterhouse chops from the middle and rear.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 400 (pork); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Pork tenderloin
cuts.about: A small, lean, very tender muscle inside the loin.
cuts.nameNote: Not the same as pork loin.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 400 (pork); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Baby back ribs
cuts.about: Ribs from the top of the rib cage where they meet the loin. Shorter and leaner than spare ribs.
cuts.nameNote: “Baby” describes the shorter rib, not a young pig.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 400 (pork); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Country-style ribs
cuts.about: Meaty strips from the shoulder end of the loin (or from the butt). Often have little or no rib bone.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 400 (pork); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Spare ribs (St. Louis)
cuts.about: Ribs from the belly side of the rib cage. St. Louis-style are spare ribs trimmed square.
cuts.nameNote: “Pork ribs” alone could be spare, baby back or country-style.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 400 (pork); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Pork belly
cuts.about: The fatty underside below the loin. Fresh, it’s pork belly; cured and smoked, it’s bacon.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 400 (pork); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Bacon (and pancetta)
cuts.about: Cured (and usually smoked) pork belly. Pancetta is Italian cured belly, not smoked.
cuts.nameNote: “Canadian bacon” and back bacon are cured loin, not belly.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 400 (pork); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Fatback (lardo)
cuts.about: The firm fat layer over the loin. Cured with herbs, it’s lardo.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 400 (pork); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Ham (fresh or cured)
cuts.about: The hind leg. Fresh ham is uncooked and uncured; most “ham” is cured and often smoked. Prosciutto, jamón and country ham are dry-cured legs.
cuts.nameNote: “Ham” alone doesn’t say fresh or cured. A cured ham’s name may name a style or region; Ibérico refers to the breed.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 400 (pork); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Ham hock (shank)
cuts.about: The lower leg joint, usually smoked, used for long cooking. Hocks also come from the front leg.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 400 (pork); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Pork jowl (guanciale)
cuts.about: The cheek and jaw. Cured, it’s guanciale.
cuts.source: USDA IMPS Series 400 (pork); NAMI Meat Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Chicken breast
cuts.about: The chest muscle. Sold bone-in or boneless; a cutlet is a breast sliced or pounded thin.
cuts.source: USDA Poultry Products specifications (IMPS P-Series); NAMI Poultry Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Airline breast (Statler)
cuts.about: A boneless breast with the first wing joint (the drumette bone) left on.
cuts.source: USDA Poultry Products specifications (IMPS P-Series); NAMI Poultry Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Chicken tenders
cuts.about: The small strip of muscle under the breast (the tenderloin).
cuts.nameNote: “Strips” and “fingers” may be tenderloins or breast meat cut to shape.
cuts.source: USDA Poultry Products specifications (IMPS P-Series); NAMI Poultry Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Wing
cuts.about: The whole wing: drumette, flat and tip. Party wings are wings split into drumettes and flats.
cuts.source: USDA Poultry Products specifications (IMPS P-Series); NAMI Poultry Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Drumette
cuts.about: The meaty first wing section, attached to the body. Looks like a small drumstick but is wing.
cuts.source: USDA Poultry Products specifications (IMPS P-Series); NAMI Poultry Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Flat (wingette)
cuts.about: The middle wing section with two thin bones.
cuts.source: USDA Poultry Products specifications (IMPS P-Series); NAMI Poultry Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Thigh
cuts.about: The upper leg. Dark meat; sold bone-in or boneless.
cuts.source: USDA Poultry Products specifications (IMPS P-Series); NAMI Poultry Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Drumstick
cuts.about: The lower leg. Dark meat.
cuts.nameNote: “Chicken leg” can mean the drumstick alone or the whole leg.
cuts.source: USDA Poultry Products specifications (IMPS P-Series); NAMI Poultry Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Leg quarter
cuts.about: The thigh and drumstick together, often with part of the back.
cuts.source: USDA Poultry Products specifications (IMPS P-Series); NAMI Poultry Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Chicken oyster
cuts.about: Two small, tender pieces of dark meat on the back, near the top of each thigh.
cuts.source: USDA Poultry Products specifications (IMPS P-Series); NAMI Poultry Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Back
cuts.about: The backbone and ribs, mostly used for stock.
cuts.source: USDA Poultry Products specifications (IMPS P-Series); NAMI Poultry Buyer's Guide

cuts.name: Whole chicken
cuts.about: The whole bird. Spatchcocked means backbone removed and flattened; a half chicken is split down the middle.
cuts.nameNote: Poussin and Cornish game hen are young, small chickens; USDA class names (Broiler, Roaster, Cornish game hen) set an age range.
cuts.source: USDA Poultry Products specifications (IMPS P-Series); NAMI Poultry Buyer's Guide
